gen-creation.story: Genesis opens with the earth empty and dark, and God speaking light into being. Over six days the account moves from light to sky, from land and seas to plants, from sun, moon and stars to creatures of the water, air and ground, and last to people, made in God's image. God calls what he has made good, and the seventh day is set apart for rest. Chapter 2 then slows down to a garden in Eden, where God places the man to work it and care for it.
gen-creation.why: It frames everything that follows: the world is made on purpose and called good, and people are given a place in it with meaning.

gen-ark.story: Genesis says the earth had filled with violence, and God told Noah to build a large ark. Noah, his family and the animals went in, and floodwaters covered the earth for a long time. When the water went down, the ark came to rest in the mountains of Ararat, and Noah sent out a raven and a dove to learn whether the ground was dry. After they left the ark, God promised never again to flood the whole earth and set a rainbow in the clouds as the sign of that promise.
gen-ark.why: The rainbow is a sign of a promise made to every living thing, a reminder in this story that mercy outlasts judgment.

gen-abram-stars.story: Abram, later called Abraham, was called to leave his home for a land God would show him, with a promise that his family would become a great nation. Years passed and he still had no child. One night God took him outside and told him to look at the stars and count them if he could, saying his descendants would be as many. Abram believed the promise, and the text says God counted that belief to him as righteousness.
gen-abram-stars.why: It shows trust as the heart of faith: Abram believed before he could see anything come of it.

gen-ladder.story: Jacob was leaving home alone, running from his brother Esau's anger after taking Esau's blessing. At night he lay down with a stone for a pillow and dreamed of a stairway that reached from earth to heaven, with angels going up and down on it. God stood above it and repeated the promise made to Abraham and Isaac, adding that he would be with Jacob wherever he went. Jacob woke and said God was surely in this place, and he named it Bethel, which means house of God.
gen-ladder.why: Jacob was on the run and by himself, and the dream says God's presence meets people even there.

exo-bush.story: Moses was looking after sheep near Mount Horeb when he saw a bush that was on fire but was not burning up. As he stepped closer, God called to him from the bush and told him to take off his sandals, because the ground was holy. God said he had seen the suffering of his people in Egypt and was sending Moses to bring them out. Moses protested that he was the wrong person for the task, and God answered by promising to be with him.
exo-bush.why: God's call comes to someone who feels unqualified, and the answer is his presence, not Moses' qualifications.

exo-red-sea.story: After leaving Egypt, the people found the sea in front of them and Pharaoh's army behind them. Moses stretched out his hand, and through the night a strong east wind drove the sea back, so the Israelites crossed on dry ground with walls of water on either side. When the Egyptian army followed, the water returned and covered them. Moses and the people then sang in praise to God for the rescue, and Miriam led the women with a tambourine.
exo-red-sea.why: It is the great rescue of the Old Testament, the story the people return to when they need to remember that God brings freedom.

exo-sinai.story: In the third month after leaving Egypt, the people camped at the foot of Mount Sinai. God told Moses he would meet them there, and the people spent two days preparing. On the third morning there was thunder and lightning, a thick cloud and a very loud trumpet blast, and the whole mountain was wrapped in smoke because the Lord had come down on it in fire. Moses went up the mountain to speak with God.
exo-sinai.why: It is where Israel is given the law and the covenant, and where they begin to be shaped as a people who belong to God.

exo-tablets.story: At Sinai, God spoke the Ten Commandments to the people. They begin with God, who brought Israel out of Egypt, and call the people to have no other gods, to make no idols or images to worship, and not to misuse God's name. They go on to keep the Sabbath day and honor father and mother, and they forbid murder, adultery, stealing, lying about a neighbor and coveting what belongs to someone else. Later in Exodus the words are written on two tablets of stone.
exo-tablets.why: They are a short picture of what it means to love God and to love your neighbor, and later writers keep returning to them.

jos-jericho.story: After crossing into the promised land, Israel came to Jericho, a city shut up tight behind its walls. God gave Joshua unusual instructions: march around the city once a day for six days, with seven priests blowing trumpets in front of the ark of the covenant. On the seventh day they marched around seven times, the priests sounded the trumpets, the people shouted, and the walls fell.
jos-jericho.why: The victory comes through trust and obedience to God's word, not through the strength of the army.

rut-harvest.story: After her husband died, Ruth stayed with her mother-in-law Naomi and traveled with her from Moab to Bethlehem. It was the barley harvest, and Ruth went out to glean, gathering the grain the reapers left behind, in the field of a man named Boaz. Boaz had heard of her loyalty to Naomi and made sure she had enough to eat and was safe. The book ends with Boaz marrying Ruth, and the family line that follows leads to King David.
rut-harvest.why: It is a quiet story of loyalty and kindness, showing God's care at work through ordinary harvests and families.

1sa-goliath.story: Israel's army faced the Philistines across a valley, and for forty days a giant named Goliath challenged anyone to fight him. No one dared, until David, a young shepherd who had come to bring food to his brothers, stepped forward. Saul offered him armor, but David took his staff, his sling and five smooth stones from the stream instead. He told Goliath he came in the name of the Lord, and one stone from his sling brought the giant down.
1sa-goliath.why: The story is told as a victory that depends on God, not on size or weapons.

1ki-temple.story: After David, his son Solomon became king and, in the fourth year of his reign, began to build the temple in Jerusalem. The work took seven years and used cedar, stone and gold. When it was finished, the priests brought the ark of the covenant into it, and a cloud filled the house. Solomon stood before the people and prayed, asking God to hear whenever they prayed toward this place.
1ki-temple.why: The temple was the center of Israel's worship, and Solomon's prayer shows the hope of a place where people meet God and are heard.

1ki-carmel.story: Under King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, many in Israel had turned to the god Baal. The prophet Elijah called the people to Mount Carmel and set a challenge: each side would prepare a sacrifice and call on their god to send fire. The prophets of Baal called from morning until evening and nothing happened. Elijah had water poured over his sacrifice and altar three times, offered a short prayer, and fire fell and burned up everything. The people fell down and said that the Lord is God.
1ki-carmel.why: The scene asks the people to choose whom they will trust, and it is still a story about divided loyalties.

psa-shepherd.story: This short psalm, described as a psalm of David, pictures God as a shepherd and the writer as a sheep who lacks nothing. The shepherd leads him to green pastures and quiet waters, restores his soul and guides him along right paths. Even in the darkest valley, he says, he will not be afraid, because the shepherd is with him. The psalm ends with a table prepared, goodness following him all his life, and a home in the house of the Lord.
psa-shepherd.why: People have turned to it in grief and in fear for centuries as a reminder that they are not alone.

psa-lamp.story: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, a poem in praise of God's word. It is an acrostic, arranged by the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and every verse in a section of eight begins with that section's letter. The writer uses many names for God's word, such as law, commands, decrees and promises. He says it is a lamp for his feet and a light for his path, and he asks God to help him keep it, even in trouble.
psa-lamp.why: It shows Scripture as daily guidance: a lamp lights the next few steps, not the whole road at once.

dan-lions.story: Daniel served under King Darius, who planned to put him over the whole kingdom. Jealous officials tricked the king into signing a law that anyone who prayed to anyone but the king for thirty days would be thrown to the lions. Daniel kept praying to God as he always had, three times a day at his open window. Darius was distressed, but the law could not be changed, and Daniel was put in the lions' den with a stone sealed over it. At dawn the king hurried back and found Daniel unharmed, because God had shut the lions' mouths.
dan-lions.why: It shows steady, daily faithfulness holding up under pressure, and it ends with the king honoring God.

jon-fish.story: God told Jonah to go to the city of Nineveh and warn it, but Jonah boarded a ship heading the other way. A great storm came, and Jonah told the sailors to throw him overboard, and the sea grew calm. A great fish swallowed him, and Jonah spent three days and nights inside it, praying, before it spat him out onto dry land. Jonah then went to Nineveh, the people turned from their evil, and God showed them mercy, which made Jonah angry.
jon-fish.why: The book ends with a question about God's compassion for people we might not expect, and it leaves the answer to the reader.

mat-manger.story: Matthew begins with the family line of Jesus, then tells how Mary was found to be expecting a child through the Holy Spirit before she and Joseph were married. Joseph was a just man and planned to end the engagement quietly. An angel came to him in a dream and told him to take Mary as his wife and to name the child Jesus. Matthew connects this with the words of a prophet, that a virgin would have a son called Immanuel, which means God with us. The manger itself appears in Luke's account of the birth.
mat-manger.why: Matthew presents the birth as the beginning of God with us, a promise carried by an ordinary family.

mat-star.story: After Jesus was born in Bethlehem, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem asking where the newborn king of the Jews was, because they had seen his star rise. King Herod was troubled, and the priests told him the prophets pointed to Bethlehem. The star went ahead of the wise men until it stopped over the place where the child was. They knelt and worshipped him and gave gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh, then went home another way after a warning in a dream not to return to Herod.
mat-star.why: People from far away come to honor the child, a first sign in Matthew that this story is for everyone.

mat-baptism.story: John the Baptist was preaching in the wilderness near the Jordan, calling people to turn from their sins and baptizing those who did. Jesus came from Galilee to be baptized by him, and John at first objected, saying he needed to be baptized by Jesus instead. Jesus said it was right to do this, and John agreed. As Jesus came up out of the water, the heavens opened, the Spirit of God came down like a dove, and a voice from heaven said this was his beloved Son.
mat-baptism.why: It marks the start of Jesus' public work and describes God's approval of him.

mat-nets.story: Walking beside the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw two brothers, Simon called Peter and Andrew, casting a net into the lake, because they were fishermen. He told them to follow him and said he would make them fish for people. They left their nets at once and followed him. A little farther on he called two more brothers, James and John, who were mending nets in a boat with their father, and they also left and followed.
mat-nets.why: It shows the first followers answering a simple invitation by leaving ordinary work behind.

mat-sermon.story: Jesus went up on a mountainside, sat down, and began to teach his disciples while a crowd listened. He started with blessings for the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the gentle, those who hunger for what is right, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers and those who are persecuted. He told his listeners that they were salt and light for the world, and he spoke about love for enemies. The teaching continues through chapters 6 and 7, with guidance on prayer and on building a life on his words.
mat-sermon.why: Often called the Sermon on the Mount, it is the best-known summary of how Jesus calls his followers to live.

mat-calm-sea.story: Jesus got into a boat with his disciples to cross the Sea of Galilee. A violent storm came up, so that the waves swept over the boat, while Jesus was asleep. The frightened disciples woke him and said they were about to die. He asked why they were afraid, then got up and spoke to the wind and the waves, and everything became completely calm. The disciples were amazed and asked what kind of man even the winds and the sea obey.
mat-calm-sea.why: The disciples' question is one the Gospel invites every reader to think about and answer.

mat-parables.story: Jesus sat by the lake, and because the crowd was so large he taught from a boat. He told stories, called parables, about everyday things. In the best known, a farmer scatters seed that falls on the path, on rocky ground, among thorns and on good soil, and only the good soil produces a crop. Jesus later explained that the seed is the message of the kingdom and the soils are the ways people receive it. Other parables in the chapter compare the kingdom to a mustard seed, to yeast, to hidden treasure and to a valuable pearl.
mat-parables.why: Parables invite listeners to think about how they listen and about what is worth giving everything for.

mat-loaves.story: A large crowd had followed Jesus to a quiet place, and by evening they were hungry. The disciples suggested he send the people away to buy food, but Jesus told them to give the people something to eat. They had only five loaves and two fish. Jesus looked up to heaven, gave thanks, broke the loaves and handed them to the disciples to pass around. Everyone ate and was satisfied, and twelve baskets of leftovers were gathered up.
mat-loaves.why: A small offering placed in Jesus' hands becomes more than enough, and the disciples have a part in the giving.

mat-entry.story: As Jesus and his disciples came near Jerusalem, he sent two of them to bring a donkey and her colt, and he rode into the city. Many in the crowd spread their cloaks and branches on the road and shouted praise to the Son of David. Matthew says this fulfilled the words of a prophet about a king coming humbly on a donkey. The whole city was stirred and asked who he was, and the crowds said he was the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.
mat-entry.why: It shows what kind of king he is: arriving in humility, not with weapons, only days before the cross.

mat-last-supper.story: On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, Jesus ate the Passover meal with his twelve disciples in Jerusalem. He told them that one of them would betray him. During the meal he took bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to them, saying it was his body. Then he took a cup and said it was his blood, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. They sang a hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives.
mat-last-supper.why: Many churches remember this meal in communion, each in their own way, and see in it Jesus giving himself for others.

mat-cross.story: Jesus was handed over to Pilate, who, under pressure from the crowd, gave the order for him to be crucified. Soldiers mocked him and led him out to a place called Golgotha, where he was crucified between two criminals. Darkness covered the land for three hours, and at about the ninth hour Jesus cried out and gave up his spirit. At that moment the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom, and a Roman centurion said that truly this was the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathea then laid his body in a new tomb.
mat-cross.why: Christians read the cross as the center of the story, where Jesus gives his life for others.

mat-tomb.story: After the Sabbath, at dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to look at the tomb. There was an earthquake, and an angel rolled back the stone and told the women that Jesus was not there, because he had risen, as he had said. The angel sent them to tell the disciples, and on the way Jesus met them and greeted them. Later, on a mountain in Galilee, he told his disciples to go and make disciples of all nations, and promised to be with them always.
mat-tomb.why: The resurrection is the hope on which Christian faith rests: death is not the last word.

luk-shepherds.story: On the night Jesus was born, shepherds were out in the fields near Bethlehem, keeping watch over their flocks. An angel appeared to them and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified. The angel told them not to be afraid, because a Savior had been born that day, and that they would find the baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger. A crowd of angels praised God, and the shepherds hurried to Bethlehem, found Mary, Joseph and the baby, and told everyone what they had heard.
luk-shepherds.why: The news first reaches ordinary working people, something Luke takes care to point out.

luk-prodigal.story: Jesus told a story about a father with two sons. The younger son asked for his share of the inheritance, left for a distant country and spent it all, and ended up hungry, feeding pigs. He decided to go home and ask to be taken on as a servant. While he was still far off, his father saw him, ran to him, embraced him and held a feast. The older son, who had stayed home, was angry, and the father went out to plead with him as well.
luk-prodigal.why: It pictures forgiveness as being met on the road before the apology is finished, and it leaves open whether the older brother comes in.

jhn-cana.story: Jesus, his mother and his disciples were guests at a wedding in Cana in Galilee when the wine ran out. The mother of Jesus told him about it and then told the servants to do whatever he said. He had them fill six large stone water jars with water, then draw some out and take it to the master of the feast. It had become wine, and the master remarked that the best had been kept until last. John calls this the first of Jesus' signs, and says his disciples believed in him.
jhn-cana.why: John begins the signs at an ordinary celebration, showing Jesus caring about joy in everyday life.

act-pentecost.story: Jesus' followers were together in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost when a sound like a rushing wind filled the house. What looked like tongues of fire rested on each of them, and they were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages. Visitors from many nations, gathered in the city, heard them talking about the wonders of God in their own languages. Peter stood up and explained what was happening, and about three thousand people were baptized that day.
act-pentecost.why: The gift crosses language barriers, and it marks the beginning of the church's life and mission.

act-damascus.story: Saul was on his way to Damascus to arrest followers of Jesus when a light from heaven flashed around him and he fell to the ground. A voice asked why he was persecuting him, and when Saul asked who was speaking, the voice said it was Jesus. Saul got up blind and was led into the city, where for three days he did not eat or drink. The Lord sent a disciple named Ananias to him, and Ananias objected, because of what Saul had done to believers, but he went, laid hands on Saul, and Saul could see again and was baptized. He soon began telling people in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.
act-damascus.why: Saul, later known as Paul, turns from opponent to messenger, an example of a life turned around.

1co-love.story: Paul wrote to the church in Corinth, which was divided and proud of its spiritual gifts. In this chapter he says that speaking in angelic tongues, knowing every mystery, or giving everything away means nothing without love. He then describes love as patient and kind, not envious or boastful, not self-seeking and not easily angered. It rejoices in the truth, and it bears and endures all things. He ends by saying that faith, hope and love last, and that love is the greatest of the three.
1co-love.why: It is often read at weddings, yet it was written to a quarreling congregation, so it is about how people treat one another every day.

heb-faith.story: This chapter describes faith as trusting in what we hope for, even though we cannot see it. It then walks through the Old Testament, naming people who acted on God's promises, among them Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham and Sarah, Moses and Rahab. Some saw great victories and others suffered, and the chapter says they did not receive everything promised in their own lifetimes. It leads into the next chapter's call to run the race with perseverance.
heb-faith.why: It gives a long line of ordinary, flawed people who trusted God, which makes faith feel shared and handed down.

rev-throne.story: John writes that he saw a door standing open in heaven and heard a voice calling him up to see what must happen. He describes a throne with someone seated on it, a rainbow like an emerald around it, flashes of lightning and a sea like glass. Around the throne were twenty-four elders on thrones, and four living creatures who never stop praising. The elders lay their crowns before the throne and say that God is worthy of glory, honor and power, because he created all things.
rev-throne.why: Before the visions of struggle, the book shows worship at the center of everything, with God reigning.

rev-new-jerusalem.story: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, because the first heaven and earth have passed away. He sees the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven, prepared like a bride dressed for her husband. A loud voice announces that God will make his home among his people and wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death, mourning, crying or pain. The one on the throne says that he is making everything new.
rev-new-jerusalem.why: The Bible's story ends with God making his home with people and healing what was broken.

rev-river-tree.story: In the last chapter, John is shown a river of the water of life, clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God down the middle of the city's street. On each side of the river stands the tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit, a crop each month, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations. There will be no more curse, and God's servants will see his face. The book closes with an invitation to come and a promise that Jesus is coming soon.
rev-river-tree.why: It echoes the garden of Genesis at the very end, so the Bible opens and closes with a place of life and healing.
